editor_spans.body: The Prime Minister stood on the site of Ravenscraig and told the story of Scottish centralisation as if it began at Holyrood. He said Scotland is 'the most devolved nation in the UK' and yet 'one of the most centralised nations in Europe', and that devolution 'was never supposed to stop at the doors of the Scottish Parliament'. Neither he nor the government's preview of the speech mentions that the regional tier he now wants rebuilt existed until the 1990s, and that Westminster abolished it. From 1975 the college's site sat inside Strathclyde Regional Council, which covered half of Scotland's people and ran transport, strategic planning, education and economic development across the whole Clyde city region. A Conservative government at Westminster legislated in 1994 to replace Strathclyde and the other regions with smaller single-tier councils. It did this partly because a Labour-run regional authority was a rival power base. The Scottish Parliament inherited a map with no middle tier.

Holyrood made things worse. It took the police and fire services into national bodies, froze council tax for years, and ring-fenced council budgets. But the speech's own logic points the other way from the blame it implies. A decision taken 'hundreds of miles away' closed Ravenscraig, and decisions taken in London also removed the regional government that could have organised the response. The City Region Deals the Prime Minister praises were set up to fill that gap. They are Treasury-negotiated bargains, not standing powers, which is why they feel like something that needs 'what comes next'. The honest version of his offer is that he is asking Edinburgh to rebuild what London dismantled. Framed that way, the Scottish Government would have a harder time turning it down as a Westminster raid.

The concrete item in the offer, 'DWP devolution' of employment support, is also older ground than the speech suggests. The Smith Commission settlement after 2014 already handed Holyrood contracted employability programmes, and the Scottish Government built its own services on that, through Fair Start Scotland and then No One Left Behind. What stayed in London was the core: Jobcentre Plus, conditionality and sanctions, which are the 'computer says no' face of the state that the speech complains about. The test of whether the 'Easterhouse principle' can go nationwide is whether that reserved core moves. Another layer of local schemes added on top of it would not pass that test. The speech promises the principle but never says which DWP functions are actually on the table.
